sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Napoleon crossed the Neman into Russia on 24 June 1812 with the largest army Europe had seen, expecting the campaign to be over within 30 days. Heavily outnumbered, the Russian command decided to retreat, and Napoleon failed to separate or destroy the two western armies under Barclay de Tolly and Bagration.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: France and Russia had drifted apart since Tilsit over the Continental System, Napoleon's Austrian marriage and his annexation of Oldenburg, and both prepared for war from 1811. Austria and Prussia sent contingents but told Alexander they would make no serious effort; Sweden had come to terms with Russia, and Russia made peace with Turkey in May 1812.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Napoleon aimed at the strategic envelopment of the Russian army and needed a rapid, decisive victory. After failing to separate the Russian armies, he moved on Smolensk, one of Russia's most sacred cities, hoping the Russians would stand there. They did, partly because Barclay's junior officers threatened mutiny if he did not.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Smolensk stands on the Dnieper, about 370 km west of Moscow. Its old defences were aged and dilapidated, its suburbs lay outside the walls, and the Russians' line of retreat ran across the river.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon's main army included the corps of Ney and Davout and Murat's cavalry. Barclay de Tolly commanded the Russian First Western Army and the united forces, with Bagration's Second Army. Strengths given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Bagration joined Barclay at Smolensk at the beginning of August. Napoleon, whose march on Vitebsk had failed to separate them, turned south-east and crossed the Dnieper on the night of 13–14 August, with Ney's infantry and Murat's cavalry leading.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The French columns marched to within about 50 km of Smolensk under constant Cossack harassment before meeting serious resistance. On 14 August a stubborn Russian rearguard at Krasnoi gave the Russians time to man the city's defences. The French appeared before Smolensk on 16 August and on the 17th took the suburbs, with Davout in the centre, but the assault stalled against the walls while French artillery reduced much of the city to burning ruins. Early on 18 August the Russians withdrew across the river, destroying the bridges and firing the town; a rearguard of ten regiments held as the first French troops broke in. On 19 August Ney and Murat defeated the Russian rearguard at Valutina, but the main army escaped.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Having brought the Russians to battle at Smolensk, Napoleon attacked the city and intended to encircle its defenders. Barclay defended the city, then, anticipating the encirclement, ordered a withdrawal by night. Napoleon halted at Smolensk until 25 August before continuing east.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The night withdrawal of 17–18 August decided the battle: the Russians gave up the city but kept their army.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The French took Smolensk, but the mass of the Russian army eluded pursuit; the Fondation Napoléon timeline notes that Napoleon did not press the pursuit after Valutino. The city was left in ruins, and General Gudin was mortally wounded at Valutina.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The campaign went on deeper into Russia and closer to winter. Barclay's retreat led to his replacement by Kutuzov, who was determined to fight before giving up Moscow and did so at Borodino. Long marches and supply failures, more than combat, had already taken a heavy toll of Napoleon's army, above all of its horses, for which forage was lacking.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Distance and supply wear down an invading army; an enemy who refuses to be fixed can trade ground for time; a city taken without its defenders gains little.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources date the battle 16–18 August (Britannica) or 15–17 August (the Fondation Napoléon timeline), and Kutuzov's appointment to 17 or 18 August. Linden describes a bitter dispute between Davout and Murat over Murat's reckless attacks in the pursuit. Losses are given differently and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Since crossing the Neman in June 1812 Napoleon had failed to bring the Russian armies to a decisive battle, and after Smolensk they continued to retreat toward Moscow. Barclay de Tolly was replaced by Kutuzov, whose popularity with the army had brought him the command and who was determined to fight a major battle before abandoning Moscow.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Napoleon still needed the rapid, decisive victory that had eluded him, hoping it would bring Alexander to terms. For the Russians, Moscow carried a political weight that made giving it up without a battle hard to accept.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Kutuzov halted the retreat near Borodino, about 110 km west of Moscow, and hastily built fortifications to block the road to the city. Napoleon meant to destroy the Russian army; fearing that an attempt to outflank it might fail and let it escape, he chose a frontal attack.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Russian line was concentrated between Borodino and Semenovskoe, near the Moskva, with the old Smolensk road behind it. Its key works were the V-shaped earthworks known as Bagration's flèches and the central Raevsky redoubt. The front was about five kilometres long.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon's army included the corps of Davout, Ney and Eugène, Murat's cavalry, Poniatowski's Poles and the Imperial Guard. Kutuzov commanded the united Russian armies, with Bagration's Second Army on the left. Strengths are given in the sources but not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 5 September Murat's advance guard and Davout's troops fought for the forward Russian position at Shevardino, on the Russian left, while Poniatowski took Doronino to the south. At a council that evening Davout proposed a wide flanking march with his corps round the Russian left; Napoleon judged it too risky and approved only a small diversion by Poniatowski. The 6th was spent concentrating the army, reconnoitring and preparing.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The French attacked at about 6 a.m. on 7 September. Eugène's troops took Borodino on the Russian right. Davout and Ney attacked the flèches, held by Vorontsov and Neverovsky; the works changed hands for about three hours until Ney took them around 10 a.m. Davout was wounded and handed his command to Murat, and Bagration was gravely wounded. The French then turned on the central redoubt, which was taken and lost repeatedly; Montbrun was mortally wounded and Auguste de Caulaincourt, who replaced him, was killed. By noon the French artillery began to tip the scales, but the attacks could not overwhelm the Russian resistance. In the afternoon both armies were exhausted, and the battle subsided into a cannonade that lasted until nightfall.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon rejected Davout's flanking plan for a frontal attack. During the battle, distant from the smoke-covered field and perhaps unsure of the situation, he refused to commit the Imperial Guard; his marshals were divided, with Murat, Davout and Ney in favour of committing it and Berthier, Duroc and Bessières against. Kutuzov committed every available man, withdrew during the night and, at a council at Fili on 13 September, decided to abandon Moscow to save the army.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Because Kutuzov had nothing left in reserve, Britannica judges that Napoleon's refusal to commit the Guard forfeited the chance of a decisive rather than a narrow victory.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Kutuzov withdrew during the night; his army was badly mauled but survived. Losses on both sides were very heavy, and the sources' figures differ. Bagration died of his wound on 24 September. The French held the field but did not win the decision Napoleon wanted.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Murat's troops reached Moscow on 14 September and Napoleon entered the nearly deserted city; fires broke out and destroyed much of it, and their origin is uncertain. The Russians refused to come to terms, and after waiting a month Napoleon began his retreat on 19 October. He later made Ney prince de la Moskowa.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A battle won on the field may not win the campaign; the decision to commit the last reserve weighs the present battle against the rest of the campaign; a frontal attack gives up the chance of a decisive manoeuvre in exchange for certain contact.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon chronology notes that historians still debate what committing the Guard would have achieved. Napoleon's entry into Moscow is dated 14 September (Britannica) or the morning of 15 September (the chronology, which has Murat arrive on the 14th). The Russian forward position at Shevardino is described as a redoubt in many accounts but not in the sources read. Casualty figures differ widely and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After a month in Moscow, with the Russians refusing to come to terms, Napoleon began his retreat on 19 October 1812. At Maloyaroslavets on 24 October he found Kutuzov in his path and chose to return by the direct road through Mozhaisk and Smolensk, over ground already devastated.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Napoleon had tried to avoid any appearance of retreat by first ordering a march on Kaluga. By late November three Russian armies were converging on his line: Wittgenstein from the north, Chichagov from the south and Kutuzov's main army behind.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Napoleon needed to get the army across the Berezina before the Russian armies closed on it; the Russians had the chance to trap it against the river.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Berezina crossed the army's road at Borisov, where the bridge was the vital crossing. Upstream, a peasant guided the French to a ford near Brillowo and Studianka, where the river was some 40 to 50 m wide; beyond it the road west led through the marshes of Zembin.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: West of Orsha the remnant of the Grande Armée was joined by the corps of Victor and Oudinot from the northern flank; behind the combatants marched a mass of stragglers. General Eblé commanded the pontonniers. Against them were Chichagov's army on the far bank, Wittgenstein's approaching from the north and Kutuzov's main army following. Strengths given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Britannica notes that most of the army's losses occurred before the first snowfall. At Krasnoi in mid-November Kutuzov declined a general engagement, and Ney's rearguard escaped only across the breaking ice of the Dnieper. The advance guard reached the Berezina on 23 November to learn that Chichagov held the Borisov bridge; Oudinot retook Borisov, but the Russians burned the bridge as they withdrew. On 24 November Corbineau's cavalry found the ford at Studianka.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Eblé's pontonniers reached Studianka on the afternoon of 25 November and, working in the icy water, built two trestle bridges from the timbers of the village houses, one for troops and one for wagons and guns, while feints at Borisov and downstream drew Chichagov's attention south. On 26 November Oudinot's corps crossed; the second bridge opened in the afternoon, and ice floes repeatedly damaged both, forcing repairs in the water. The Guard and the main body crossed on 27 November, but most of the stragglers waited for daylight. On 28 November Victor held off Wittgenstein on the east bank while Oudinot and Ney contained Chichagov on the west bank; Partouneaux's division, cut off near Borisov, surrendered. At 9 a.m. on 29 November the bridges were set on fire as Cossacks reached the bank.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon chose to cross upstream at Studianka and deceived Chichagov with feints at Borisov and farther south. Chichagov concentrated at Borisov, and the force he had left opposite Studianka stayed silent and then withdrew. The order to burn the bridges, carried out two hours later than Napoleon had ordered according to Ganière, protected the army but abandoned those still on the east bank.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Russians' failure to contest Studianka on 25 and 26 November let the bridges be built and the first troops cross unopposed.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The core of the army escaped across the Berezina and through the marshes toward Zembin. Many thousands of stragglers, sick and wounded were left behind when the bridges burned; Ganière writes that those who could walk were taken prisoner and the others killed. The army had escaped destruction, but as a fighting force it was finished.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The march went on in extreme cold to Vilnius and Kovno, where only a few broken thousands recrossed the Neman. On 5 December, after news of the Malet conspiracy, Napoleon left the army to Murat and hurried to Paris. The cavalry destroyed in Russia could not be replaced, and the French army could no longer absorb new recruits into well-established formations. The exhausted Russians halted at the Vistula.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Deception and engineering can open an escape route even in catastrophe; a rearguard that holds both banks buys time for the main body; the cost of a retreat falls heaviest on the stragglers, the sick and the wounded.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Russian coordination failed: Chichagov was deceived, Ganière describes Kutuzov's army as largely inactive on 28 November, and Britannica notes that Schwarzenberg had failed to pursue Chichagov. The burning of the bridges, with so many still on the east bank, remains a painful question. Dates differ slightly: Ganière places the first snow on 3 November and Ney's escape on 18 November, Britannica the first snowstorm on 6 November. The losses of the campaign are estimated very differently and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: The destruction of the Grande Armée in Russia brought Prussia into the war. Yorck's Convention of Tauroggen on 30 December 1812 was followed by the Russo-Prussian alliance of Kalisz in February 1813 and Prussia's declaration of war in March. The French fell back from the Vistula to the Elbe, abandoning Dresden.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Austria, under Metternich, moved toward armed mediation, and on 26 April the king of Saxony undertook to join Austria if war came. Napoleon hoped to recover Germany before Austria could intervene.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Napoleon raised a new army of hastily trained conscripts. He planned to march on Leipzig, outflanking the Allies, then turn south to drive them against the Erzgebirge. Wittgenstein, commanding the Allies, aimed to cut off Ney's flank guard at Lützen, split the French and drive the Army of the Elbe back on the Elster.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought on the plain south-west of Leipzig, around the villages of Gross-Görschen and Kaja near Lützen, between the Saale and the Elster.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon's forces were divided into the Army of the Main under his own command and the Army of the Elbe under Eugène; Ney's corps formed the flank guard at Lützen, with Bertrand and Macdonald among the other commanders. The Allies under Wittgenstein were grouped south of Leipzig; Scharnhorst was chief of staff to Blücher. The French were very short of cavalry, while the Allies had numerous cavalry; other figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 1 May Napoleon entered Lützen. Ney was to remain there to protect the movement on Leipzig and the approach of the rear corps, but he disposed his troops carelessly and did not reckon with an Allied attack. The Allies stood south of Leipzig, almost at right angles to the French line of operations.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 2 May the Allies opened their cannonade at Gross-Görschen, surprising Ney's corps while Napoleon was overseeing the attack on Leipzig. The Prussians bore much of the fighting, the Russians joining later. Napoleon ordered his troops to concentrate at Kaja and re-established the front while waiting for Bertrand to come in on the Allied left and Macdonald to cut their retreat to the Elster. Both came slowly; as French numbers began to tell, nightfall ended the fighting, and Wittgenstein withdrew in good order, covered by his cavalry.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon turned the army away from Leipzig to concentrate at Kaja and tried to envelop the Allies with Bertrand and Macdonald. Wittgenstein chose to attack the French flank on the march.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The concentration at Kaja turned the battle; the slow arrival of the flanking corps and the onset of night kept it from becoming decisive.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The French held the field, but the victory was inconclusive and costly. Without cavalry Napoleon could not pursue, and the Allies retreated in order toward Dresden and Bautzen. Scharnhorst was wounded and died of the wound at Prague on 28 June.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The Allied retreat led the king of Saxony to abandon them, and his army joined the French. Napoleon entered Dresden on 8 May and reorganised his forces there before marching on the Allies at Bautzen.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A rebuilt army can win battles, but without cavalry victories cannot be exploited; a carelessly posted flank guard invites attack; an envelopment depends on corps arriving in time.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica calls the victory inconclusive and gives the French heavier losses than the Allies; the Fondation Napoléon timeline says nightfall saved the Allies from a debacle. Britannica criticises Ney's dispositions, while Hourtoulle's biography notes only that Ney held important commands at Lützen and Bautzen. Figures differ and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Lützen the Allies retreated through Dresden; the Russians fell back to the Spree, and the Prussians rejoined them at Bautzen. Napoleon entered Dresden on 8 May and spent over a week reorganising his forces, sending Eugène to Italy and dividing the armies between himself and Ney.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Saxony had returned to the French alliance, and Austria was preparing armed mediation. Bülow's Prussian corps covered Berlin, and Napoleon set up his base at Dresden for operations against both the main Allied army and Berlin.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: On 18 May Napoleon set out for Bautzen to seek a decisive battle. He would attack the Allied front on 20 May; on the 21st Ney, coming from the north, would strike their flank and rear, cut their communications and push them toward the Erzgebirge. The Fondation Napoléon timeline describes the plan as an attempt to repeat Friedland.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The Allies held a position on the Spree around Bautzen, east of Dresden. Ney's approach from the north led toward Preititz, behind the Allied right.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon commanded the main army in person; Ney led the northern wing. Wittgenstein commanded the Allies, who were far superior in cavalry although Napoleon had the larger army; Barclay replaced Wittgenstein on 29 May. Figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Napoleon first ordered Ney to send two of his corps toward Berlin, then countermanded the order and summoned all of Ney's forces to Bautzen; the new instructions arrived too late to bring them all together.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 20 May Napoleon's preliminary attack on the Spree succeeded. On 21 May Ney reached Preititz but let himself be drawn into an inconclusive fight with the Allied right wing; the timeline says he attacked the Allied centre instead of the crumbling right. The limited reach of Ney's outflanking movement and the Allies' superior cavalry let them break off and retreat eastward from 4 p.m.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon's plan depended on Ney driving deep behind the Allies; Ney turned toward the fighting instead. The Allies chose to retreat in time rather than risk envelopment.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Ney's halt around Preititz decided the outcome: the envelopment never closed, and the Allies escaped.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The French won the field again, at heavier cost than the Allies. The timeline quotes the Saxon officer Baron von Odeleben describing the Allied retreat as a masterpiece of tactics. Duroc was mortally wounded on 22 May. The Allies crossed the Katzbach on 26 May and turned south to protect Silesia.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: On 4 June both sides accepted the armistice of Pläswitz, later extended to 10 August. Napoleon counted on rebuilding his cavalry; the Allies used the pause to bring in the Prussian Landwehr and, at Reichenbach, to agree that Austria would enter the war if Napoleon rejected its terms. Austria declared war on 12 August.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: An envelopment depends on subordinates who understand the intent; orders changed late may not reach their recipients in time; a victory without pursuit leaves the enemy free to recover.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon timeline calls the armistice Napoleon's great mistake, arguing that he could have pressed his advantage; Britannica stresses that his offensive had spent its force and his army lacked ammunition, supplies and cavalry. Ney's conduct is described differently: Britannica says he was drawn into an inconclusive encounter, the timeline that he attacked the wrong part of the line. Figures differ and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: During the armistice the Allies agreed at Reichenbach that Austria would enter the war if Napoleon refused its terms. The armistice ended on 10 August 1813 and Austria declared war two days later.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Allies divided their forces into three armies: Schwarzenberg's Army of Bohemia, accompanied by the Russian and Prussian monarchs, Blücher's Army of Silesia and Bernadotte's Army of the North. They agreed to avoid battle with Napoleon himself and to attack his subordinates. Schwarzenberg became commander-in-chief of the Allied armies.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Allies hoped to capture Dresden, Napoleon's main base of operations and supply depot. Napoleon meant to stand on the defensive in the south while seeking a decision in the north against Berlin; he did not know that the Army of Bohemia had been greatly reinforced.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Dresden, the Saxon capital on the Elbe, was the base of Napoleon's defence of the Elbe line. Schwarzenberg attacked in a great semicircle around the city, his flanks resting on the river; Pirna, upstream, lay on the Allied line of retreat into Bohemia.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Gouvion-Saint-Cyr held Dresden with a small garrison and built many fortifications. Napoleon brought up the Guard and other corps, joined on the night of the 26th by Marmont and Victor. Schwarzenberg commanded the Austrian, Prussian and Russian Army of Bohemia. On the first day the French were heavily outnumbered; figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: In mid-August Napoleon moved east against Blücher, who retreated before him. On 23 August he learned that the advance of the Army of Bohemia had forced Gouvion-Saint-Cyr back on Dresden; leaving Macdonald to hold Blücher, he hurried west and ordered Vandamme toward Pirna. The danger at Dresden was such that he sent most of his forces straight to the city, and the Guard entered Dresden at 10 a.m. on 26 August after marching 145 km in 72 hours.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Schwarzenberg, who had meant to attack at 4 p.m., decided to retire, but too late to stop the battle from starting. On 26 August the Allies attacked around the city; Gouvion-Saint-Cyr's defenders gave ground slowly, and in the late afternoon Napoleon drove the Allies back to their starting positions. On 27 August, from 6 a.m., in rain and mud, the French drove back the Allied right and overwhelmed the left, which had become detached from the centre. The mobility of the French artillery told when infantry and cavalry could hardly move. At 4 p.m. the Allies withdrew in disorder.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon's decision to break off his move against Blücher and march back to Dresden at speed saved the city. On the second day he attacked both Allied wings. Schwarzenberg's decision to call off the attack came too late.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Guard's arrival and Napoleon's counterattack on the afternoon of 26 August turned the battle; the collapse of the Allied left on the 27th decided it.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Allies withdrew with heavy losses, but their retreat was not pressed hard. Napoleon fell ill on 28 August and returned to Dresden, leaving the pursuit to his corps commanders. Britannica calls Dresden his last major victory in Germany.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Defeats of Napoleon's subordinates soon undid the victory: Oudinot at Grossbeeren on 23 August, Macdonald on the Katzbach on 26 August, Vandamme surrounded at Kulm on 29–30 August and Ney at Dennewitz on 6 September. The Fondation Napoléon timeline says Kulm greatly boosted Allied morale.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A coalition that refuses battle with the strongest commander and attacks his subordinates can win without winning his battles; interior lines let a commander strike in turn, but only if his subordinates can hold; a victory without pursuit can be undone within days.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica judges the autumn campaign the worst conceived and most disastrous of Napoleon's career, tying him to the fortresses on the Elbe. Both Napoleon's illness and the shortcomings of his corps commanders are given as reasons the victory was not exploited. The Fondation Napoléon's biography of Schwarzenberg dates the battle 25–26 August, against 26–27 August in Britannica and the Fondation's timeline. Losses differ and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica's article on the battle and its narrative of the autumn campaign give the course of events; the Fondation Napoléon's 1813 timeline adds the Allied left and Kulm, and its biography of Schwarzenberg his command.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Dresden, the defeats of Napoleon's subordinates at Grossbeeren, the Katzbach, Kulm and Dennewitz wore down his army. Bavaria made an armistice with the Allies on 17 September 1813 and joined them by the Treaty of Ried on 8 October. In early October Blücher crossed the Elbe at Wartenburg and Bernadotte at Rosslau.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Napoleon's German allies were wavering: Bavaria's change of side led Württemberg to follow and began the collapse of the Confederation of the Rhine. The Allied armies threatened his line of communications through Leipzig.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Operating on interior lines, Napoleon first tried to defeat Blücher and Bernadotte but failed to catch Blücher at Düben. He then planned to attack the Army of Bohemia once Schwarzenberg had committed it near Leipzig. The Allies aimed to converge on him there from several directions.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Leipzig in Saxony was ringed by villages that became battlefields: Wachau, Liebertwolkwitz and Gossa to the south, Schönefeld and the suburbs to the north. The Elster and Pleisse ran to the south and west, and the French line of retreat westward crossed the Elster by a single bridge.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon concentrated his army at Leipzig, leaving Gouvion-Saint-Cyr at Dresden. The Allied armies were commanded by Schwarzenberg, Blücher, Bennigsen and Bernadotte; Austrians, Prussians, Russians and Swedes fought in their ranks, and Schwarzenberg was commander-in-chief. The French were outnumbered; figures are given in the sources but not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 14 October Napoleon ordered his troops to Leipzig. Early on 16 October he was still waiting for Macdonald when, at 9 a.m., Schwarzenberg opened his attack on the heights of Wachau.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 16 October Napoleon held off Schwarzenberg's attacks from the south and Blücher's from the north but defeated neither; the fighting at Liebertwolkwitz, Wachau and Gossa ended roughly as a draw, and Murat's cavalry charge came to nothing. The 17th was a lull, during which Bennigsen and Bernadotte arrived. On the 18th the Allies attacked from north and south; Schönefeld fell, two Saxon divisions and the Württemberg cavalry changed sides, and after nine hours of assaults the French were pushed back into the suburbs. At 2 a.m. on 19 October Napoleon began the retreat west over the single Elster bridge; at 1 p.m. a corporal blew it up while it was still crowded with French troops, trapping the rearguard and the wounded in Leipzig. Poniatowski, made a marshal during the battle, died trying to cross the Elster on horseback.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Threatened in his communications, Napoleon concentrated at Leipzig and attacked Schwarzenberg; Britannica judges that had he been able to concentrate on 14 October, Schwarzenberg would have been exposed to defeat. The Allies used the lull of the 17th to bring up Bennigsen and Bernadotte. On the 18th, with ammunition running short, Napoleon began planning his retreat.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The failure to win on 16 October, before the other Allied armies arrived, turned the battle; the defections of the 18th and the early destruction of the Elster bridge turned a defeat into a disaster.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The French retreated west with very heavy losses: the trapped rearguard and wounded were taken prisoner, and many generals, guns and wagons were lost. Allied losses were also very heavy. The sources' figures differ and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The battle ended the French Empire east of the Rhine and destroyed what was left of French power in Germany and Poland; the Confederation of the Rhine was dissolved. Napoleon's army broke through a Bavarian force at Hanau and crossed the Rhine at Mainz in early November, with typhus among the stragglers, while many more troops remained besieged in German fortresses. For the second year in succession Napoleon had lost an army. Blücher was made a field marshal for his part in the battle.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Interior lines lose their value once converging armies are close enough to attack together; a coalition that coordinates its approach can surround a single strong commander; a single line of retreat is a mortal weakness.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The Fondation Napoléon timeline says the corporal blew the bridge while his commander was away and the bridge was under fire; Britannica describes him as frightened and the bridge as in no danger of attack. Leipzig is often described as the largest battle in Europe before the twentieth century; the sources read call it one of the most severe of the Napoleonic Wars and the Battle of the Nations. French losses are estimated very differently and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Leipzig the Allies offered peace at Frankfurt on the basis of France's natural frontiers, but withdrew the offer before Napoleon's assent arrived. They invaded France with three armies: Blücher crossed the Rhine on 31 December 1813, and Schwarzenberg came by way of Switzerland. After an engagement at Brienne on 29 January 1814, Napoleon was defeated at La Rothière on 1 February.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Allies opened the Congress of Châtillon on 5 February and demanded that France return to its frontiers of 1792. After La Rothière they agreed at Brienne to separate their armies: Blücher would march on Paris by way of Châlons and Meaux, Schwarzenberg by way of Troyes.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Leaving a force to contain Schwarzenberg, Napoleon marched against Blücher's left flank, staking everything on a last offensive with much weaker forces. He aimed to strike Blücher's dispersed corps one by one before they could unite.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Blücher's Army of Silesia advanced on Paris along the Marne valley. Napoleon struck from the south at Champaubert, between Blücher's rear at Vertus and his leading corps beyond Montmirail; Château-Thierry lay on the Marne, and Vauchamps on the road back toward Châlons.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon's small force included the corps of Marmont, Ney and Mortier and the Guard. Blücher's army included Olsufiev's Russian corps, Osten-Sacken's Russians and Yorck's Prussians. Napoleon was heavily outnumbered; figures given in the sources are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: On 8 February Blücher's main column was strung out over about 70 km, with Yorck's corps well to the north of the line of advance. Napoleon ordered Marmont to occupy Sézanne and arrived himself late on 9 February.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 10 February Marmont and Ney routed Olsufiev's isolated Russian corps at Champaubert, placing the French across Blücher's line of march. Leaving Marmont to watch Blücher, Napoleon turned west and on 11 February defeated Osten-Sacken at Montmirail before Yorck could help him. On 12 February the French drove Yorck and Sacken's remnants across the Marne at Château-Thierry. Napoleon then turned back to support Marmont, and on 14 February, at Vauchamps and that night at Étoges, the French struck Blücher's own advance as he retreated.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon chose to leave Schwarzenberg to a containing force and strike Blücher's flank, and at each stage he left a corps to hold one part of Blücher's army while he struck another. Blücher's advance with his corps widely spread exposed them to defeat in turn.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Champaubert, which put the French between Blücher's separated corps, made the rest of the campaign possible.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: In four days Blücher's army was scattered and lost several times as many men as the French. But Blücher rallied his divisions around Châlons, and by 18 February, reinforced, his army had largely recovered its strength. Britannica judges that Napoleon had spent himself and his troops to achieve only a postponement of defeat.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Napoleon turned against Schwarzenberg and took the Seine crossing at Montereau on 18 February, and Schwarzenberg withdrew toward Troyes. Encouraged by Montmirail, Napoleon demanded the Rhine and the Alps as France's frontiers, but by the Treaty of Chaumont on 9 March the four Allied powers bound themselves to fight on.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Defeat in detail can still work against a dispersed enemy, but when the enemy has more armies and reserves than the attacker has time, operational victories only postpone defeat.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica stresses how little the campaign achieved strategically. The Fondation Napoléon chronology describes the victories in detail but gives different loss figures and, in one place, a different date for Montmirail. Figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Britannica's narrative of the campaign of France gives the course of the Six Days, and its account of Schwarzenberg's advance the sequel. Marie de Bruchard's chronology for the Fondation Napoléon adds the French side, and Britannica's biography of Blücher his career.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After the Six Days, Napoleon turned south against Schwarzenberg and reoccupied Troyes on 24 February 1814. Blücher, declining to retreat with Schwarzenberg, moved north toward the Marne and the Aisne, and Bülow's and Wintzingerode's corps were transferred to his command.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: By the Treaty of Chaumont on 9 March, Britain, Russia, Austria and Prussia undertook to fight on until France accepted its old frontiers, and agreed on a 20-year alliance against any later French expansion.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Napoleon aimed to strike Blücher's rear and cut off his retreat across the Aisne. Blücher broke off his offensive and withdrew north to join Bülow and Wintzingerode; the sudden capitulation of Soissons on 3 March let him cross the Aisne safely and regroup at Laon.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Blücher regrouped behind the Aisne in a strong position at Laon. The French crossed the Aisne at Berry-au-Bac; Craonne lay on the approach, and Marmont's corps camped near Athies, where it was surprised.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon followed with the main body, with Mortier and Marmont behind him. Blücher's army, reinforced by Bülow and Wintzingerode, was far larger; figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Napoleon crossed the Aisne at Berry-au-Bac and ran into Blücher's flank guard at Craonne.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 7 March a confused and bloody encounter at Craonne lasted into the night; Napoleon held the field and Blücher fell back to Laon. On 9 March Napoleon, attacking from the south in two columns, failed against the strong position. That night Marmont's corps was surprised near Athies and broken up by Allied cavalry; it was rallied only at Berry-au-Bac the next day. Napoleon withdrew to Soissons.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon chose to attack a much larger army concentrated in a strong position. After the night attack, Blücher fell ill and the Prussians halted their pursuit, which Britannica says kept the reverse from being worse.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The night attack on Marmont's camp ended any chance of success at Laon.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Napoleon withdrew to Soissons. Craonne had cost both sides heavily, and the defeats caused desertions from the French army.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Napoleon then retook Reims from a Russian corps, but he could no longer stop either Allied army. Schwarzenberg meanwhile pushed Macdonald and Oudinot back toward Provins.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Repeated offensives with dwindling forces wear out the attacker; a careless night camp invites surprise; a weaker army cannot beat a concentrated enemy in a strong position.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Britannica calls Craonne a confused and bloody encounter with roughly equal losses; the Fondation Napoléon chronology says Napoleon held the field. Britannica attributes the limited pursuit after Athies to Blücher's illness and the Prussian halt. Figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Laon and Reims, Napoleon could no longer stop either Allied army. Schwarzenberg had pushed Macdonald and Oudinot back toward Provins.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: The Allies had bound themselves at Chaumont on 9 March to fight on until France accepted its old frontiers, and the talks at Châtillon had stalled.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Napoleon marched from Reims toward Méry-sur-Seine to attack Schwarzenberg's communications. Schwarzenberg withdrew toward Troyes on the news of his approach and gathered his forces between the Seine and the Aube.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Arcis-sur-Aube is a town on the Aube, which there had only one bridge; Napoleon crossed the river and fought with it at his back.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon crossed the Aube with a small force; Schwarzenberg had nearly twice as many men on the first day and far more on the second. Figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: By 19 March Schwarzenberg's forces stood between the Seine and the Aube, and Napoleon crossed the Aube at Arcis.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 20 March Napoleon pushed Schwarzenberg's forces off the battlefield by nightfall. On 21 March Schwarzenberg resumed the attack with his whole army, and Napoleon had to retreat across the Aube; Schwarzenberg failed to destroy the only bridge, which let him withdraw.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Too weak to stop either Allied army, Napoleon resolved to move east to rally his garrisons in Lorraine, provoke a general rising and throw himself on Schwarzenberg's rear. On 23 March Tsar Alexander learned of unrest in Paris from an intercepted letter, and at a council at Sompuis on 24 March the Allies decided to advance directly on Paris instead of following him.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Allies' decision at Sompuis to ignore Napoleon's threat to their communications and march on Paris decided the campaign.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: Napoleon broke off the battle and withdrew across the Aube. Losses on the first day were about equal; figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Marmont and Mortier were beaten at La Fère-Champenoise on 25 March and could not stop the Allies. After a day's fighting before the city, Paris capitulated in the early hours of 31 March, and the Allies entered it that day. The Senate deposed Napoleon, his marshals refused to fight on, and Marmont took his corps over to the Allies; Napoleon abdicated and, by the Treaty of Fontainebleau, received the sovereignty of Elba.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A manoeuvre against the enemy's communications fails when the enemy aims at the political centre instead; a commander must weigh the safety of his capital as well as his army.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Whether Napoleon expected to meet only part of Schwarzenberg's army at Arcis is not stated in the sources read. The Fondation Napoléon chronology describes the intercepted letter as supposedly from Savary. The Treaty of Fontainebleau is dated 11 April (the chronology) or 13 April, when Napoleon accepted it (Britannica). Figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Napoleon returned from Elba in March 1815. The Allies declared him an outlaw and recalled their armies for a fresh invasion of France. In Belgium a Prussian army under Blücher and a mixed British, German and Dutch-Belgian army under Wellington were preparing an offensive, which Blücher had planned with Wellington for the end of June.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Napoleon expected the Allies to advance on Paris only after mid-July and chose to strike first in Belgium, before their armies could unite. Many of his generals refused to serve him, and opinion in France was divided.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: Napoleon aimed to keep the Prussian and Anglo-allied armies apart and defeat each in turn. On 15 June he crossed the Sambre; on 16 June he meant to take Sombreffe and the Quatre-Bras crossroads, separating the two armies. Blücher, promised support by Wellington, hoped to hold until Anglo-Dutch troops could strike the French left.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Blücher's army held a line from Saint-Amand through Ligny to Sombreffe, behind the Ligne stream; Ligny and Saint-Amand were fortified villages. At the Quatre-Bras crossroads, to the west, Ney faced Wellington's troops.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon attacked with Gérard's and Vandamme's corps and Grouchy's cavalry, keeping the Imperial Guard in reserve; Ney commanded the left wing at Quatre-Bras, which included d'Erlon's corps. Blücher commanded the Prussian army with Gneisenau as his chief of staff; Bülow's corps did not arrive in time. Figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: At a meeting at the windmill of Bussy at 1 p.m., Wellington and Blücher concluded that Napoleon was about to attack at Ligny, and the Prussians accepted battle there. Napoleon watched from the Naveau windmill at Fleurus.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: The attack began around 3 p.m. Gérard met fierce resistance in Ligny, while Vandamme took and lost Saint-Amand under Prussian counterattacks; Blücher fed in his reserves wherever the line was threatened. Around 6 p.m. a column approaching the French left was taken for the enemy, delaying Napoleon's attack; it was d'Erlon's corps, which then marched back toward Quatre-Bras and fought in neither battle. At about 7.30 p.m., after a heavy bombardment, the Guard and Milhaud's cuirassiers broke the Prussian centre at Ligny. In the cavalry fighting that followed Blücher was thrown and pinned under his horse, and French cuirassiers passed him in the dark. At Quatre-Bras Ney fought Wellington to a standstill.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Napoleon divided his army between two wings and tried too late to draw d'Erlon to Ligny; Tsas holds him responsible for letting the political aim of reaching Brussels override military principles. After the battle Gneisenau chose Wavre, to the north, as the rallying point rather than a line of retreat east toward Prussia; Britannica says Blücher withdrew toward Wavre to ensure cooperation with Wellington, at risk to his own communications. Napoleon refused Grouchy's request to pursue that night.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The Guard's attack won the battle, but the retreat toward Wavre rather than east decided the campaign by keeping the Prussians within reach of Waterloo.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Prussians were beaten but withdrew in good order, holding parts of Brye and Sombreffe through the night. Quennevat calls Ligny a half-victory, closer to Eylau than to Austerlitz. Losses were heavy on both sides; figures are not repeated here.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Because of the defeat at Ligny, Wellington had to fall back from Quatre-Bras toward Waterloo. Grouchy was sent after the Prussians the next day but was slowed by a storm; Blücher reached Wavre, and two days later his troops marched to Waterloo and appeared on the French right flank at a critical stage of the battle.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Defeat is not destruction; the choice of a line of retreat can be a strategic decision; lost or conflicting orders can cost a decisive result.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: Responsibility for d'Erlon's wasted march is disputed: d'Erlon said he was shown a pencilled note diverting him to Ligny; Tsas blames Vandamme's misreading of the column and, above all, Napoleon's division of his forces, while others cited by Tsas see a failure of liaison. Accounts of Blücher's fall differ, as the Fondation Napoléon's close-up notes. Britannica criticises both Ney and Grouchy for failing to destroy either Allied army while they were separated. Figures differ and are not repeated here.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Jean-Claude Quennevat's and François Tsas's articles in the Revue du Souvenir Napoléonien give the course of Ligny and of Quatre-Bras; the Fondation Napoléon's close-up on Blücher, the National Army Museum and Britannica add the campaign and Blücher's decisions.

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: Napoleon returned from Elba in 1815. A new coalition mobilized against him.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: His advance into Belgium sought to separate Wellington's and Blücher's armies before larger coalition forces arrived.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The French needed a rapid decision; the Allies needed to sustain cooperation despite separate command structures.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: Wellington held the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge with forward strongpoints including Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Napoleon faced Wellington's multinational army and, later, Blücher's Prussian corps.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: Much Allied infantry sheltered behind the crest of the ridge, out of sight and partly protected from artillery. Squares formed against the later cavalry attacks.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: Attacks on the strongpoints and center were followed by cavalry assaults, Prussian intervention and the final Guard attack.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Wellington chose to stand with promised Prussian support. Blücher marched toward him after the defeat at Ligny.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: Prussian pressure forced Napoleon to divide attention and reserves. The Imperial Guard's repulse preceded general French retreat.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The coalition won on 18 June. Napoleon's attempt to restore his rule failed.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: The campaign ended with Allied occupation of Paris and Napoleon's final exile.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: Coalition cooperation can be an operational capability. Study liaison and marching decisions alongside the actions visible on the battlefield.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: National narratives assign credit differently, including the weight given to the Prussian intervention. The schematic simplifies simultaneous engagements and is not derived from period maps.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: Compare the National Army Museum narrative with Royal Armouries and the Prussian-focused Fondation Napoléon dossier. The National Archives holds three 1815 plans of the battle (MPH 1/387); they are catalogued but not digitised.

perspectives.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
perspectives.objective: Defeat Wellington before the coalition armies could combine effectively.
perspectives.known: Ligny had forced a Prussian retreat, but its direction and recovery remained critical.
perspectives.uncertainty: How much Prussian force could reach the battlefield in time.
perspectives.constraints: Wet ground, elapsed time and competing demands for reserves.
perspectives.decision: He continued the attack while allocating troops to the Prussian threat. The account describes actions, not an invented inner monologue.
perspectives.forces: The Army of the North, strong in artillery and cavalry, with the Imperial Guard as a final reserve. Grouchy's wing had been detached to follow the Prussians.
perspectives.terrain: Rain-soaked ground delayed the attack and hampered artillery and cavalry. Fortified farms broke up assaults before they reached the ridge.
perspectives.logistics: The campaign had to succeed quickly, before larger coalition armies reached France's frontiers.
perspectives.outcome: Defeat ended his return to power. Debate continues over the late start, Grouchy's movements and the use of the cavalry and the Guard.

perspectives.name: Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington
perspectives.objective: Hold the position until Prussian assistance could make a combined victory possible.
perspectives.known: Blücher had promised support; his arrival depended on a difficult march.
perspectives.uncertainty: The timing and scale of reinforcement.
perspectives.constraints: A mixed army, an extended defensive line and repeated French pressure.
perspectives.decision: He defended the ridge and strongpoints, then advanced as the French attack failed.
perspectives.forces: A multinational army of British, Dutch-Belgian, Hanoverian, Brunswick and Nassau troops of uneven experience.
perspectives.terrain: The Mont-Saint-Jean ridge sheltered infantry behind its crest. Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte broke up attacks in front of the line.
perspectives.logistics: His communications ran north toward Brussels and the coast. Contact with the Prussians was essential to the plan.
perspectives.outcome: A combined Allied victory. British national narratives long underplayed the Prussian contribution.

perspectives.name: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher
perspectives.objective: Restore cooperation with Wellington after Ligny.
perspectives.known: Wellington intended to fight near Waterloo.
perspectives.uncertainty: March delays and the situation when each corps arrived.
perspectives.constraints: Reorganization after defeat and routes from Wavre.
perspectives.decision: He committed corps toward Waterloo. Their intervention turned a two-army encounter into a coalition victory.
perspectives.forces: Prussian corps regrouping after Ligny. Bülow's corps, which had not fought at Ligny, led the march to Waterloo.
perspectives.terrain: Muddy lanes slowed the march from Wavre. Plancenoit became the focus of the Prussian attack on the French right.
perspectives.logistics: Retreating north to Wavre after Ligny, rather than east toward Prussia, kept the army in reach of Wellington while it regrouped.
perspectives.outcome: The Prussian attack and pursuit turned the French defeat into a rout. Some national narratives have underestimated this role.
